title: COMP 4736 · Part 4
subtitle: Threads: why they exist, the word processor and web server, the classical thread model, Pthreads, user-space, kernel and hybrid implementations, Java platform and virtual threads, pop-up threads
description: Part 4 of Rahim Oraji's lectures (Tanenbaum Ch. 2): a thread as a flow of execution with its own program counter, registers and stack; the four motivations (10–100 times faster to create than a process); the word processor with three threads and the dispatcher/worker web server with the three ways to construct a server; the classical model's per-process and per-thread items, each thread's own stack and the four thread states; the six Pthreads calls and the instructor's two-thread demo with pstree and /proc/<pid>/task; user-level versus kernel-level threads with their advantages and problems and the slide's comparison table; hybrid many-to-one, one-to-one and many-to-many; Java threads by extending Thread, implementing Runnable and a lambda, and virtual threads; pop-up threads. Ends with a mock midterm section and the closed-book recall drill.
intro:
:::quiz What the exam asks here
Mostly definitions and comparisons: shared versus private items, the problems of user-level threads (blocking system calls, no clock interrupts within a process), what the kernel can do when a kernel thread blocks, the three hybrid mappings, and the Pthreads call names. The practice paper's own key says thread switching costs more with user-level threads; the slide says user-level switching is faster (no trap, no context switch). Know both.
:::
